newsitem.title: CANADA: Peru halts bold police action after Tokyo pressure.
newsitem.headline: Peru halts bold police action after Tokyo pressure.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, under pressure from Tokyo over bold police manoeuvres outside the Japanese mission in Lima, on Saturday pledged to halt any "potentially risky acts" endangering hostages' lives.

He also condemned four policemen whose lewd gestures drew gunfire last Monday from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) in the first direct assault on security forces during the 46-day-old hostage crisis.
"What I wish to say is that four police officers engaged in a provocative act, that certainly was not timely and appropriate," Fujimori told a news conference, with Hashimoto at his side.
"Therefore we should like to see to it that such acts will not be repeated."
After the MRTA fired at police, Hashimoto told Peru to exercise caution to avoid "accidents or incidents." He and Fujimori then agreed to hold the Toronto summit to narrow down strategy differences.

Peru's increasingly aggressive police moves outside the ambassador's residence heightened Japanese concern over the safety of the hostages, among whom are about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
Apparently responding to this concern, Fujimori told the news conference: "Of course, any potentially risky (police) acts should be excluded."
Police stepped up their war of nerves on the rebels Jan. 23 to wear down the roughly 15 MRTA guerrillas holding the 72 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence.

They sent convoys rumbling past the residence at least five times, blasted martial music at odd hours and buzzed the residence with helicopters and planes. Special forces commandoes, toting automatic weapons, scrambled to the compound's walls.

Although Fujimori said he planned to keep police in the area, his pledge to curb their actions appeared to be one of the few public Peruvian concessions to Japan in the Toronto summit, which began informally on Friday night.

The appointment of a Japanese envoy to the mediating commission to end the crisis, might be another. The envoy would allow Japan to play a role in the negotations and may be asked for advice, Hashimoto said.

In the post-summit news conference on Saturday, Fujimori disclosed that Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a close friend of the president's, handled unofficial working documents on talks between the MRTA and the government.

Cipriani, also a member of the mediating commision, has been a frequent visitor to the Japanese ambassador's residence, repeatedly celebrating Mass there and accompanying Red Cross representatives on their visits.

"There have been documents, unofficial working drafts (of talks between the rebels and the government), that have been within the pastoral work of Cipriani." Fujimori said, without indicating who drew up the papers.
